conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how moms are feeling emotionally in the first weeks and months after birth.  

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team; we simply want to make sure you feel heard and supported. We’ll walk through 10 gentle questions about the past seven days—no right or wrong answers, just whatever is true for you today. Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.

To start:  
Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?
Honestly... I’ve noticed it’s been harder to laugh lately. I still do sometimes, but it feels like I have to make myself, and the joy doesn’t last long. Mostly I’m too tired or just not in the mood.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not as much as I used to. I’ll smile if something’s really funny, but it feels kind of forced—like I’m doing it because I know I should, not because it comes naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom says she’s coming over or when I manage a hot shower—but they fade fast. Mostly I’m just focused on getting through the next feeding, the next diaper change.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… sometimes. Like, the other night she wouldn’t settle for two hours and I kept thinking maybe I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate something that bothers her, or I’m holding her wrong. I know babies cry, but I still catch myself thinking it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little. Most of the worry is about her—like, is she breathing okay, is she getting enough milk—but even when everything looks fine, I still feel this knot in my stomach that something could go wrong. It’s not constant, but it pops up several times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

There have been a couple of moments—usually when she’s sleeping longer than I expect—where my heart races and I feel shaky, thinking something’s wrong even though she’s right there and fine. It passes after a minute, but it leaves me on edge.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—some days it feels like the dirty bottles, the laundry, the night feedings just pile up faster than I can handle. I’ll start one chore, the baby cries, and suddenly I’m near tears because I can’t keep up. Most of the time I manage, but I end the day exhausted and overwhelmed.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I do have trouble falling or staying sleep, but it’s more because my mind keeps ticking through her schedule—when will she wake, is she warm enough—than because I’m feeling desperately unhappy. Once I drift off I’m usually okay unless she cries.
I have felt sad or miserable

I get waves of sadness, mostly in the evenings when I’m alone with her and everything feels quiet. It’s not all day, but a few times this week I just sat there rocking her with tears in my eyes, not even sure why.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried like that. I’ve teared up a couple of times, but I haven’t had those big, can’t-stop tears.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I couldn’t do that to my baby or to my family.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant ≈ weeks old)  
Date: ___  
Clinician: ___  

Symptoms endorsed  
• Diminished ability to laugh/enjoy activities (Q1, Q2)  
• Recurrent self-blame/guilt over normal infant behavior (Q3)  
• Unwarranted anxiety/worry several times daily, brief panic episodes when infant sleeps (Q4, Q5)  
• Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks, tearful when interrupted (Q6)  
• Evening waves of sadness, occasional tearfulness (Q8)  
• Sleep disturbance linked to intrusive worries rather than pure mood distress (Q7)  

Denies  
• Persistent crying spells (Q9)  
• Any self-harm ideation (Q10)  

Pattern  
Mild-to-moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms, situational overwhelm, no safety concerns.  

Screening significance  
Meets partial criteria for postpartum depression and/or postpartum anxiety; does not currently indicate high-risk depression with self-harm. Continue monitoring, consider formal EPDS/PHQ-9 and referral for psycho-education/support within 1–2 weeks.
